To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the activity of rats in a 6-arm maze is characterized by a high level of exploratory activity in the arms of the maze and a low level of locomotor activity in the central part of the maze.
the patterns of brain metabolic activities of rats that were allowed to explore a familiar maze configuration and those that were exposed to an unfamiliar maze configuration differed significantly.

experienced rats explored the radial maze more efficiently than nonexperienced rats and showed a different metabolic activity in prefrontal cortex, cingulate cortex and thalamus than nonexperienced animals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the brain activity in the prefrontal cortex and thalamus is related to exploratory behavior in a radial maze.

the question of whether rats exposed to a novel environment explore it in an optimal manner, i.e., in an efficient way, and whether they are capable of using the information gained from the exploration to solve problems in the future.
the development of new methods for measuring the metabolic activity in the rat brain, which is based on a combination of a radial maze and 2-deoxy[3H]glucose.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the 2-deoxy-glucose method is a valuable tool for the study of brain function.

the 2-deoxy[3H]glucose uptake patterns of the experienced rats are not different from those of the nonexperienced rats, except for the hippocampus, where the experienced animals showed a higher uptake.
2-deoxy-glucose uptake patterns in the brain of rats exploring a 6-arm maze are different between experienced and non-experienced rats.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
rats with experience in a 6-arm tunnel maze show a higher efficiency of maze exploration, but not an increased locomotor activity.
2-deoxy-D-glucose uptake in the rat brain is influenced by the animal's previous experience with the maze.
the 2-[3H]-deoxyglucose technique is a valuable tool in studies of brain metabolism and that the 6-arm maze is a useful tool in studies of learning and memory.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is not a static entity, but is constantly in motion and is constantly changing.

the brain activity patterns of rats that had been trained in a 6-arm maze were different from those of rats that had not been trained in the maze, even though the rats were exposed to the same environment.
2-deoxy-glucose uptake in the prefrontal cortex and cingulate cortex is associated with spatial memory.
